vignette: Mateo Rivera was twenty-three when a documented engineering failure caused the concrete support pillars on the northbound expressway to buckle, sending his sedan and a dozen others into a tangled pile of twisted metal and shattered glass. He remembers the sound first—a grinding roar that vibrated through the steering wheel before the world tilted. He managed to crawl from his wreckage, blood from a gashed forearm staining his shirt, and turned toward the adjacent driver’s side where a woman’s door wouldn’t release. For forty minutes, Mateo pulled at the jammed handle, shouting over the hiss of ruptured fuel lines, until responders finally pried the frame open. She survived, but the silence that followed the chaos left him staring at his own hands. He had come to believe that if only he had known exactly which tool to use or which angle to pry, the outcome would have been different. The memory of that exact failure sits permanently behind his ribs. In the months that followed, his days contracted into careful routines. He found himself rereading emergency manuals and tracing alternate versions of that afternoon, asking himself how his life would have unfolded if the highway had remained intact. What frightened him most was the sheer unpredictability of the people around him. He was certain that anyone could become a threat without warning, that safety was an illusion maintained only by constant vigilance. He reached a quiet conclusion that nothing good could happen to him anymore and that he was merely waiting for the next collapse. Alongside these thoughts, certain habits took root. He stopped watching television entirely, muted news alerts on his phone, and scrolled past any article or film depicting collisions, treating every headline like a live wire. He avoided police vehicles when driving, changing lanes or taking service roads to keep marked cruisers out of his sightline. These patterns occupied his waking hours without merging into one another; they simply coexisted as the landscape of his days. Now twenty-four and working as a QA engineer in a glass-walled tech office, Mateo’s environment became the stage where these patterns played out. During his morning commute, he routed himself miles off the interstate to avoid highway overpasses, a detour that added forty minutes to his day but kept his chest from tightening. Inside the office, casual breakroom conversations quickly became difficult. When a junior developer once recounted a terrifying multi-car pileup from a weekend road trip, Mateo felt the floor seem to drop away. His vision narrowed as the room began to feel detached and unreal. He had left the kitchenette before the story finished, citing a urgent bug ticket he had to chase. He declined invitations to group dinners after colleagues began debating crash safety ratings, and he missed two team retrospectives because he could no longer stomach the commute across the city. The distance between Mateo and his coworkers widened until he found himself eating lunch alone in his car, parked in the far corner of the garage. At work, his test coverage remained meticulous, but his silence in stand-up meetings drew quiet concern from his manager. What finally brought him to the clinic was not a single breaking point, but the slow realization that he was no longer living in his own city, only navigating around it. He wants to know if the weight of that broken barrier can ever be put down, if he can sit through a conversation about a car accident without the world dissolving, and if there is still a path forward that does not require him to brace for the next collapse.
